payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Pilot Court) Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
payload.holding: The Tribunal held the insurance company liable to pay compensation to the three injured claimants after deducting 50% for contributory negligence due to driving without a license and helmets.
payload.ratio: In motor accident claim cases under Section 166 of the MV Act, the standard of proof is based on preponderance of probabilities, and police record documents such as the FIR and charge sheet are sufficient to establish negligence in the absence of rebuttal. Furthermore, contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet.

args.question: Precedents dealing with fake, forged, expired or otherwise invalid driving licences and their effect on insurance liability

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149. Where originally the licence was fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover from the insured. In own-damage claims, the insurer is not liable.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly addresses fake/forged driving licence scenarios. Distinguishes between third-party claims (where pay-and-recover applies) and own-damage claims (where insurer is absolved).
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the Supreme Court's definitive statement on fake licences. It establishes the critical distinction between third-party and own-damage claims — a distinction that governs the entire law on this subject.
supporting.quote: Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Consolidates the entire line of Supreme Court authority (Skandia, Sohan Lal Passi, Kamla, Lehru, Swaran Singh) holding that third-party liability is statutory and cannot be defeated by licence defects.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides a comprehensive synthesis of the law. The insurer must pay third parties first and then recover — even for fake/invalid licences.
supporting.quote: The liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and recover from the owner to protect third-party rights.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident. Tribunal found fundamental breach but applied pay-and-recover principle citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: Illustrates the modern Tribunal practice: even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach (no licence at all), the third-party claimant is protected via pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: The petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driving licence had expired on the date of accident but was renewed later. The court held the insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that an expired licence (as opposed to a fake one) is treated more leniently — it may not even be a fundamental breach if the driver had held a valid licence earlier.
supporting.quote: The insurance company is liable to pay the compensation as the breach of condition of the policy had not been proved.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The insurer is not primarily liable but must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Licence expired on 30.04.2008, accident on 02.07.2008, renewed on 04.07.2008. Under Section 15 proviso, renewal operates prospectively only.
supporting.why_it_matters: Clarifies the operation of Section 15 proviso — a lapsed licence renewed after 30 days does not retrospectively cover the accident date. But pay-and-recover still applies for third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The driving license shall be renewed with effect from the date of its renewal in the event the application for renewal of a license is made more than 30 days after the date of its expiry.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no authorisation/badge for transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). The court applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the principle to licence-class mismatches — driving a transport vehicle without the proper endorsement is a breach, but third-party protection still applies.
supporting.quote: The insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver held a valid LMV licence but no endorsement to drive a Mahindra Maxi Cab (commercial vehicle). Supreme Court held insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Limits the insurer's ability to avoid liability for licence endorsement issues — if the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle, lack of a commercial endorsement does not absolve the insurer.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence with transport vehicle endorsement but not the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle. Pay-and-recover ordered.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that licence endorsement deficiencies do not defeat third-party claims — the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.quote: In case of Third Party risks the Insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and is entitled to recover from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is statutory or contractual.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision comprehensively analysing the pay-and-recover principle. Holds that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: The most comprehensive Karnataka High Court authority on the point. Answers all nuances: Act policy vs contractual policy, fundamental breach vs innocent breach, fraud/collusion exception.
supporting.quote: The rule of pay and recover is applicable in view of the mandate in Section 149(4) of the Act and even if there is a breach of the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer is bound to satisfy the judgment and award as if it were a judgment debtor.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory. Absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but no special endorsement for driving a Tanker carrying hazardous goods. Pay-and-recover ordered.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the licence-defect principle to special endorsements required under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules for hazardous goods.
supporting.quote: Special endorsement is required for driving a goods carriage vehicle meant for transporting dangerous or hazardous goods... there was no such endorsement... clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of insurance policy.

supporting.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
supporting.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation, but the insurer remains liable to pay the reduced award.
supporting.fact_alignment: Claimant was driving a motorcycle without a licence and without a helmet. 50% contributory negligence deducted, but insurer still directed to pay.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even where the claimant/victim himself drove without a licence (contributory negligence), the insurer is not absolved — only the quantum is reduced.
supporting.quote: He did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Where originally the licence was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. The decision in Swaran Singh has no application to cases other than third-party risks.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claim is an own-damage claim (not a third-party claim), the insurer will cite this to argue it has no liability at all — not even pay-and-recover. The insurer will argue that the fake licence means the policy is void ab initio for own-damage purposes.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims. For third-party claims (injury/death to a pedestrian, passenger, or other vehicle occupant), the same judgment holds that the insurer must indemnify and recover. If the client's claim is a third-party claim, Laxmi Narain Dhut actually supports the client.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, and the insurer is not liable to indemnify the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite the finding that 'no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company' for breach due to no licence. The Tribunal did say the insurer is 'absolved from its liability.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Despite that language, the Tribunal ultimately applied pay-and-recover because the claimant was a third party. The insurer was directed to pay first and recover from the owner. The 'absolved' language refers to the insurer's liability to indemnify the insured, not its liability to the third-party claimant.
adverse.quote: When it is found that offending vehicle was driven by driver who was either holding no license or a fake license, then it amounts to violation of terms and conditions of policy and no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
adverse.principle: Where a driving licence has lapsed and is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, the driver does not hold a valid licence on the accident date, and the insurer is not primarily liable.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that under Section 15 proviso, a lapsed licence renewed after 30 days does not retrospectively cover the accident date, so there was no valid licence at the time of accident.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still directed pay-and-recover. The insurer's primary liability argument succeeded, but the third-party claimant was still protected. The only risk is if the client is the insured owner seeking indemnity — then this case is adverse.
adverse.quote: The driving license shall be renewed with effect from the date of its renewal in the event the application for renewal of a license is made more than 30 days after the date of its expiry.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without authorisation to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that driving a transport vehicle (taxi, maxi cab, goods carriage) without the proper licence class/endorsement is a breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The breach was established, but the third-party claimant was protected. Only adverse if the client is the insured owner resisting recovery.
adverse.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Absence of a special endorsement for driving a vehicle carrying hazardous goods constitutes a breach of policy conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the vehicle involved is a tanker or goods carriage carrying hazardous materials, the insurer will argue the driver needed a special endorsement under Rule 9 of the CMVR.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The breach was established but the third-party claimants were protected. Only relevant if the vehicle carried hazardous goods.
adverse.quote: Special endorsement is required for driving a goods carriage vehicle meant for transporting dangerous or hazardous goods.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claimant/victim was himself driving without a licence at the time of the accident, the insurer will argue contributory negligence to reduce the award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Contributory negligence reduces quantum but does not defeat the claim entirely. The insurer still pays the reduced amount. The reduction percentage depends on facts — here it was 50% because the victim also wasn't wearing a helmet.
adverse.quote: He did not have DL at the time of accident... 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

priority_arguments: Lead with the fundamental distinction: for third-party claims (injury/death to pedestrians, passengers, other vehicle occupants), the insurer's statutory liability under Section 149 is absolute — even a fake/forged/expired licence only entitles the insurer to pay and recover, not to avoid liability.
Cite Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) for the proposition that in third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover — this is the insurer's own authority turned against them.
Cite Satto (doc_033) for the comprehensive synthesis of Skandia → Sohan Lal Passi → Kamla → Lehru → Swaran Singh line of authority establishing that third-party liability is statutory.
Cite Yallavva (doc_025) for the Full Bench holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
If the licence was merely expired (not fake), cite Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) for the proposition that an expired licence may not even be a fundamental breach.
If the licence was renewed late, cite Parvathi Hebbar (doc_003) but note that pay-and-recover still applies for third-party claims.
If the issue is licence class/endorsement mismatch, cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032) for the proposition that the insurer cannot disown liability for lack of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence.
If the claimant himself was driving without a licence, argue contributory negligence (not complete defence) — cite Kamal (doc_009) for the 50% deduction precedent.
strategy.compensation_range: Depends on the facts of the specific claim (income, age, dependents). The licence defect does not affect the quantum of compensation payable to a third-party claimant — it only affects who ultimately bears the burden (insurer pays first, then recovers from owner). Use compute_quantum for the specific case facts.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect is irrelevant to quantum in third-party claims. The insurer must pay the full computed compensation and then recover from the insured. In own-damage claims, the insurer may avoid liability entirely if the licence was fake (Laxmi Narain Dhut).
risks: If the claim is an own-damage claim (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) holds that a fake licence absolves the insurer entirely — no pay-and-recover.
If the claimant/victim was himself driving without a licence, contributory negligence may reduce the award by up to 50% (doc_009).
If the insured owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed/fake-licence driver to drive, the insurer's recovery rights against the owner are stronger.

If the vehicle carried hazardous goods without the required special endorsement on the driver's licence, the insurer can argue breach (doc_001) — though pay-and-recover still applies for third parties.
If the policy is an 'Act only' policy vs a comprehensive policy, the scope of coverage may differ — though Yallavva (doc_025) holds pay-and-recover applies regardless.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For third-party claimants: file under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. The licence defect is irrelevant to the claimant's entitlement. The Tribunal should be asked to direct the insurer to pay the award in the first instance with liberty to recover from the insured owner. For insured owners facing recovery proceedings: argue that the owner took reasonable care to verify the licence (Swaran Singh test) and that the breach was not conscious or wilful.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 itself, which is the foundational Supreme Court authority on this subject. All judgments in the corpus cite and apply Swaran Singh, but the original judgment should be consulted separately.

The corpus contains no judgment from the Supreme Court directly on the question of a forged licence (as opposed to a fake licence or no licence). The distinction between 'fake' and 'forged' may be relevant in some jurisdictions.
doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) was flagged for licence defect but actually concerns Section 167 bar and workmen's compensation — not relevant to the present research.
doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal revision cases about rash driving — they do not address civil insurance liability for licence defects.

priority_arguments: Lead with the fundamental distinction: for third-party claims (injury/death to pedestrians, passengers, other vehicle occupants), the insurer's statutory liability under Section 149 is absolute — even a fake/forged/expired licence only entitles the insurer to pay and recover, not to avoid liability.
Cite Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) for the proposition that in third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover — this is the insurer's own authority turned against them.
Cite Satto (doc_033) for the comprehensive synthesis of Skandia → Sohan Lal Passi → Kamla → Lehru → Swaran Singh line of authority establishing that third-party liability is statutory.
Cite Yallavva (doc_025) for the Full Bench holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
If the licence was merely expired (not fake), cite Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) for the proposition that an expired licence may not even be a fundamental breach.
If the licence was renewed late, cite Parvathi Hebbar (doc_003) but note that pay-and-recover still applies for third-party claims.
If the issue is licence class/endorsement mismatch, cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032) for the proposition that the insurer cannot disown liability for lack of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence.
If the claimant himself was driving without a licence, argue contributory negligence (not complete defence) — cite Kamal (doc_009) for the 50% deduction precedent.
Cite Meena (doc_006) to show that post-Iyyapan, even where the driver has no licence at all, pay-and-recover applies for third-party claims.
strategy.compensation_range: Depends on the facts of the specific claim (income, age, dependents). The licence defect does not affect the quantum of compensation payable to a third-party claimant — it only affects who ultimately bears the burden (insurer pays first, then recovers from owner). Use compute_quantum for the specific case facts.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect is irrelevant to quantum in third-party claims. The insurer must pay the full computed compensation and then recover from the insured. In own-damage claims, the insurer may avoid liability entirely if the licence was fake (Laxmi Narain Dhut).
risks: If the claim is an own-damage claim (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) holds that a fake licence absolves the insurer entirely — no pay-and-recover.
If the claimant/victim was himself driving without a licence, contributory negligence may reduce the award by up to 50% (doc_009).
If the insured owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed/fake-licence driver to drive, the insurer's recovery rights against the owner are stronger.

If the vehicle carried hazardous goods without the required special endorsement on the driver's licence, the insurer can argue breach (doc_001) — though pay-and-recover still applies for third parties.
If the policy is an 'Act only' policy vs a comprehensive policy, the scope of coverage may differ — though Yallavva (doc_025) holds pay-and-recover applies regardless.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For third-party claimants: file under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. The licence defect is irrelevant to the claimant's entitlement. The Tribunal should be asked to direct the insurer to pay the award in the first instance with liberty to recover from the insured owner. For insured owners facing recovery proceedings: argue that the owner took reasonable care to verify the licence (Swaran Singh test) and that the breach was not conscious or wilful.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — The insurer was absolved because the tractor was used for non-agricultural purposes (carrying bricks/iron rods), not because of any driving licence defect. The deceased was driving a scooter without a licence, but that was the claimant's own conduct, not the insured vehicle's driver. This judgment concerns vehicle-use violations, not licence defects, and is not relevant to the present research.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — The insurer was exonerated because passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not 'third parties' under the Act policy. This judgment concerns the scope of third-party coverage (who qualifies as a third party), not licence defects. Not relevant.

doc_030 (Dadapeera) — The insurer was exonerated because the claimant was sitting on a tractor mud-guard, which violates Regulation 28 of the Rules of the Road Regulations. The court held such a person is not covered by statutory insurance under Section 147. This judgment concerns who qualifies as a covered third party, not licence defects. Not relevant.

This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 itself, which is the foundational Supreme Court authority on this subject. All judgments in the corpus cite and apply Swaran Singh, but the original judgment should be consulted separately.
doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) was flagged for licence defect but actually concerns Section 167 bar and workmen's compensation — not relevant to the present research.
doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal revision cases about rash driving — they do not address civil insurance liability for licence defects.

adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The breach was established, but the third-party claimant was protected. Only adverse if the client is the insured owner resisting recovery.
adverse.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: Absence of a special endorsement for driving a vehicle carrying hazardous goods constitutes a breach of policy conditions.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the vehicle involved is a tanker or goods carriage carrying hazardous materials, the insurer will argue the driver needed a special endorsement under Rule 9 of the CMVR.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The breach was established but the third-party claimants were protected. Only relevant if the vehicle carried hazardous goods.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claimant/victim was himself driving without a licence at the time of the accident, the insurer will argue contributory negligence to reduce the award.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Contributory negligence reduces quantum but does not defeat the claim entirely. The insurer still pays the reduced amount. The reduction percentage depends on facts — here it was 50% because the victim also wasn't wearing a helmet.

priority_arguments: Lead with the fundamental distinction: for third-party claims (injury/death to pedestrians, passengers, other vehicle occupants), the insurer's statutory liability under Section 149 is absolute — even a fake/forged/expired licence only entitles the insurer to pay and recover, not to avoid liability.
Cite Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) for the proposition that in third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover — this is the insurer's own authority turned against them.
Cite Satto (doc_033) for the comprehensive synthesis of Skandia → Sohan Lal Passi → Kamla → Lehru → Swaran Singh line of authority establishing that third-party liability is statutory.
Cite Yallavva (doc_025) for the Full Bench holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties.
If the licence was merely expired (not fake), cite Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) for the proposition that an expired licence may not even be a fundamental breach.
If the licence was renewed late, cite Parvathi Hebbar (doc_003) but note that pay-and-recover still applies for third-party claims.
If the issue is licence class/endorsement mismatch, cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032) for the proposition that the insurer cannot disown liability for lack of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence.
If the claimant himself was driving without a licence, argue contributory negligence (not complete defence) — cite Kamal (doc_009) for the 50% deduction precedent.
Cite Meena (doc_006) to show that post-Iyyapan, even where the driver has no licence at all, pay-and-recover applies for third-party claims.
strategy.compensation_range: Depends on the facts of the specific claim (income, age, dependents). The licence defect does not affect the quantum of compensation payable to a third-party claimant — it only affects who ultimately bears the burden (insurer pays first, then recovers from owner). Use compute_quantum for the specific case facts.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The licence defect is irrelevant to quantum in third-party claims. The insurer must pay the full computed compensation and then recover from the insured. In own-damage claims, the insurer may avoid liability entirely if the licence was fake (Laxmi Narain Dhut).
risks: If the claim is an own-damage claim (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) holds that a fake licence absolves the insurer entirely — no pay-and-recover.
If the claimant/victim was himself driving without a licence, contributory negligence may reduce the award by up to 50% (doc_009).
If the insured owner knowingly permitted an unlicensed/fake-licence driver to drive, the insurer's recovery rights against the owner are stronger.

If the vehicle carried hazardous goods without the required special endorsement on the driver's licence, the insurer can argue breach (doc_001) — though pay-and-recover still applies for third parties.
If the policy is an 'Act only' policy vs a comprehensive policy, the scope of coverage may differ — though Yallavva (doc_025) holds pay-and-recover applies regardless.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For third-party claimants: file under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. The licence defect is irrelevant to the claimant's entitlement. The Tribunal should be asked to direct the insurer to pay the award in the first instance with liberty to recover from the insured owner. For insured owners facing recovery proceedings: argue that the owner took reasonable care to verify the licence (Swaran Singh test) and that the breach was not conscious or wilful.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — The insurer was absolved because the tractor was used for non-agricultural purposes (carrying bricks/iron rods), not because of any driving licence defect. The deceased was driving a scooter without a licence, but that was the claimant's own conduct, not the insured vehicle's driver. This judgment concerns vehicle-use violations, not licence defects, and is not relevant to the present research.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — The insurer was exonerated because passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not 'third parties' under the Act policy. This judgment concerns the scope of third-party coverage (who qualifies as a third party), not licence defects. Not relevant.

doc_030 (Dadapeera) — The insurer was exonerated because the claimant was sitting on a tractor mud-guard, which violates Regulation 28 of the Rules of the Road Regulations. The court held such a person is not covered by statutory insurance under Section 147. This judgment concerns who qualifies as a covered third party, not licence defects. Not relevant.

This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 itself, which is the foundational Supreme Court authority on this subject. All judgments in the corpus cite and apply Swaran Singh, but the original judgment should be consulted separately.
doc_005 (L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav) was flagged for licence defect but actually concerns Section 167 bar and workmen's compensation — not relevant to the present research.
doc_016 and doc_017 are criminal revision cases about rash driving — they do not address civil insurance liability for licence defects.
